questions.q: What is the model answer's core move when a panelist asks why Alder Trust Bank's design didn't use the strongest encryption scheme on every field?
options: Restate the original, already-reasoned trade-off: the strongest scheme would block the exact-match filtering the compliance team's reporting depends on, so protection was matched to each field's actual operational use
Agree that the design was wrong and promise to change it on the spot
Deflect by saying encryption questions are outside the scope of the presentation
Claim that all fields actually do use the strongest encryption scheme
questions.explain: The answer works because it restates reasoning that was already part of the original design, not because a new justification was invented for the objection.

questions.q: In the Fenwick State University boundary-case example (a student who is also a part-time university employee), what does this lesson recommend doing when the original presentation didn't explicitly cover that case?
options: Say the design doesn't address it and move on without resolving it

Acknowledge it's a real edge case and reason through it live using the design's existing principle (legitimate educational interest), landing on an answer consistent with what's already been presented
Invent a completely new, unrelated rule on the spot to cover the case
Claim the case was already fully covered even though it wasn't
questions.explain: This mirrors Lesson 13's guidance on handling a genuinely new point honestly: reason from existing principles live rather than bluffing or leaving the gap unresolved.

questions.q: What is the Brightwell Health step-up-authentication objection ("what if the step-up provider itself goes down") really probing?
options: Whether step-up authentication is technically possible at all
Whether patients are legally allowed to view their own lab results
Whether the security control has introduced a new concentrated dependency / single point of failure, creating an availability risk
Whether Brightwell Health should remove step-up authentication entirely
questions.explain: The objection targets a risk created by the control itself (a new dependency on the step-up provider's availability), not whether the control's underlying purpose is valid.

questions.q: According to this lesson, why does a strong answer to the single-point-of-failure objection acknowledge the trade-off rather than defending the control as flawless?
options: Because admitting any flaw automatically fails a candidate
Because the panel already knows the control is flawed and will penalize any defense of it
Because step-up authentication should never be recommended in any design
Because naming the real risk and then naming a proportionate mitigation (the same pattern from Lesson 11) is more credible than claiming a security control has no downside at all
questions.explain: This reuses the 'name the risk, then name the proportionate response' pattern from risk prioritization, applied live rather than only in writing beforehand.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say a memorized, word-for-word script for a specific objection is a weaker preparation strategy than understanding the underlying design reasoning?
options: Because panels never ask the exact same question twice
Because a script only covers the exact angle it was written for, while understanding the original reasoning lets a candidate answer the same topic from an unexpected angle
Because memorized answers are automatically disqualified by review-board rules
Because scripts take longer to deliver than spontaneous answers
questions.explain: A candidate who only memorized one specific framing is caught flat when the question comes from a different angle; understanding why the choice was made transfers to any angle on the same topic.
